posts.title: Common Cents Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Common Cents Act
This bill ends the production of the penny for general circulation, requires rounding to an amount divisible by five for the payment or transfer of cash, and allows the nickel to be composed of different material.
The Department of the Treasury must stop producing the penny, except to meet collector needs. The penny shall continue to be legal tender.
Any person selling goods or services in a cash transaction, entering into other transfers of cash, or paying cash wages to an employee must round the payment up or down in accordance with the bill.
The bill also allows Treasury to discontinue the minting for circulation of any coin if Treasury follows procedures as outlined by the bill, including providing notice and a briefing to Congress.
The Federal Reserve Board must periodically report on a strategic plan for the acceptance of penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that provide services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.
Finally, the bill allows for a different material composition of the nickel. In addition to being made from an alloy of copper and nickel, the nickel may also be clad with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.
posts.committee: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
posts.meta: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee · Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-WY)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Common Cents Act would stop the U.S. Treasury from making new pennies for everyday circulation, though the Treasury could still make them to meet the needs of coin collectors. Pennies would remain legal money.

Under the bill, anyone who sells goods or services for cash, makes other cash transfers, or pays employees in cash would have to round the amount up or down so it can be divided evenly by five. This rounding rule would apply to those cash payments and transfers.

The bill also lets the Treasury stop making any coin for circulation, but only if it follows the steps set out in the bill. Those steps include giving notice to Congress and providing it a briefing.

The Federal Reserve Board would have to report regularly on a strategic plan for accepting penny orders and deposits at commercial coin terminals that offer services under agreements with Federal Reserve banks.

Finally, the bill would allow the nickel to be made from a different material. Besides the current copper and nickel alloy, a nickel could be made with an inner core of zinc and an outer layer of nickel.

posts.title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
This bill extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses and the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments.
Under current law, unreimbursed personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area (qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses) are deductible (as an itemized tax deduction or as part of the standard tax deduction) if such losses exceed $500 per casualty. A qualified disaster area is an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared during the period beginning in 2020 and ending 60 days after July 4, 2025, if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before July 4, 2025.
The bill extends the federal tax deduction for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses by defining a qualified disaster area as an area with respect to which a major disaster has been declared if the incident period begins on or after December 28, 2019, and before January 1, 2027.
The bill provides that the exclusion from gross income of qualified wildfire relief payments applies to such payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and before 2027, regardless of when such payments are received. (Currently, qualified wildfire relief payments attributable to forest or range fires declared a federal disaster after 2014 and received after 2019 and before 2026 may be excluded from gross income.)
The bill also provides statutory authority for several related tax rules.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to House
posts.committee: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee
posts.meta: Finance Committee, Ways and Means Committee · Rep. W. Steube (R-FL)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends two federal tax benefits for people affected by disasters. First, it extends the deduction for uninsured personal property losses in federally declared disaster areas. Under current law, those losses can be deducted, either as an itemized deduction or as part of the standard deduction, if each loss is more than $500. The current rules cover disasters with incident periods starting from December 28, 2019 through July 4, 2025. The bill would keep the deduction in place for disasters whose incident periods start on or after December 28, 2019 and before January 1, 2027.

Second, the bill extends the tax exclusion for certain wildfire relief payments. Such payments would not count as taxable income if they are tied to forest or range fires declared federal disasters after 2014 and before 2027. Under current law, that exclusion applies only to payments received after 2019 and before 2026. Under the bill, the timing of when the payment is received would no longer matter.

The bill also adds several related tax rules into federal law.

posts.title: Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
This bill expands a requirement for federal agencies to report expenditures on the USAspending.gov website to include other transaction agreement expenditures. (Other transaction agreements, or OTAs, are contractual instruments other than standard procurement contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements; they are exempt from many federal procurement laws and regulations).
Under current law, federal agencies must report expenditures on federal awards to USAspending.gov with the term federal award defined as federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other types of expenditures. This bill expands the definition of federal award to include expenditures under OTAs, and therefore such expenditures must be included on the USAspending.gov website.
The Department of the Treasury must ensure that data relating to OTAs are automatically transmitted to the website and a centralized view of this data is available on the website. Treasury must also annually post on the USAspending.gov website a report that includes (1) the total amount of federal spending on federal awards for which data has not been posted on the website, and (2) the reason why such spending data was not posted.
For 10 years after enactment, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must periodically submit to Congress and make publicly available a report assessing the agency's spending data and use of data standards.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House
posts.meta: Oversight and Government Reform Committee · Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL)
posts.whatsNext: Presidential review (±10 days)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill requires federal agencies to report their spending on other transaction agreements, a type of contract that falls outside standard procurement, grant, and cooperative agreement rules, to the USAspending.gov website. Currently, the reporting requirement covers federal grants, loans, cooperative agreements, contracts, and certain other expenditures, but not these agreements. Once this bill passes, spending under these agreements will count as federal awards and must appear on the site.

The Department of the Treasury must make sure data on these agreements is sent to the website automatically and that a single, central view of this data is available there. Each year, Treasury must also post a report on the site showing the total amount of federal spending on federal awards whose data has not been posted, along with the reason it was not posted.

For 10 years after the law is enacted, the Office of Inspector General of specified federal agencies must regularly send Congress a report evaluating the agency's spending data and its use of data standards. These reports must also be made available to the public.

posts.title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (90-6)
posts.summary:
Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
This bill provides continuing FY2027 appropriations for federal agencies and extends various expiring programs and authorities.
Specifically, the bill provides continuing FY2027 appropriations to federal agencies through the earlier of December 11, 2026, or the enactment of the applicable appropriations act. It is known as a continuing resolution (CR) and prevents a government shutdown that would otherwise occur if the FY2027 appropriations bills have not been enacted when FY2027 begins on October 1, 2026.
The CR funds most programs and activities at the FY2026 levels with several exceptions that provide funding flexibility or additional appropriations for various programs. For example, the CR includes exceptions for
the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC);
Small Business Administration loans;
the Disaster Relief Fund;
the Indian Health Service;
the Department of Justice; and
wildfire suppression activities.
In addition, the bill extends several expiring authorizations, including authorities and programs related to
agriculture,
flood insurance,
cybersecurity,
surface transportation,
veterans benefits,
housing,
defense production, and
trade preferences for Haiti and certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
The bill also includes provisions that
temporarily prohibit the implementation of a regulation that revises guidance for federal financial assistance,
delay the implementation of certain changes to the statutory definition of hemp,
extend the freeze on cost-of-living adjustments for Members of Congress and limits on pay increases for the Vice President and certain senior political appointees, and
provide death gratuities to beneficiaries of two Members of Congress who died while in office.
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
posts.whatsNext: Back to the House (amendments must match exactly)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill keeps the federal government funded after the new fiscal year begins on October 1, 2026, so that a government shutdown does not occur while the full set of FY2027 spending bills is still pending. It is a continuing resolution, and its funding runs through the earlier of December 11, 2026, or the date a matching appropriations act is enacted.

Most federal programs will continue at their FY2026 funding levels. A number of programs receive special treatment, with extra funding or more flexibility. These include the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), Small Business Administration loans, the Disaster Relief Fund, the Indian Health Service, the Department of Justice, and wildfire suppression.

The bill also extends several programs and authorities that would otherwise expire. These cover agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, surface transportation, veterans benefits, housing, defense production, and trade preferences for Haiti and certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

Finally, the bill includes several other provisions. It temporarily blocks a regulation that revises guidance for federal financial assistance. It delays certain changes to the legal definition of hemp. It extends the freeze on cost-of-living pay adjustments for Members of Congress and keeps limits on pay increases for the Vice President and certain senior political appointees. It also provides death gratuities to the beneficiaries of two Members of Congress who died while in office.

posts.title: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (86-11)
posts.summary:
Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
This bill imposes a variety of sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions related to Russia, extends an Iran-related sanctions law, and expands a tax deduction for teacher expenses to include early childhood educators.
For example, under the bill, the President must impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on specified persons (individuals and entities) such as the Russian president and certain Russian military commanders. The President must also increase the rate of duty up to 100% ad valorem (i.e., relative to the value) on all goods imported into the United States from a country that was among the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas if such country knowingly makes new purchases of such products after enactment of the bill.
The bill prohibits (1) the export, reexport, or in-country transfer to or in Russia of any U.S.-produced energy or energy product; (2) U.S. persons from making new investments in Russia or purchasing Russian sovereign debt; and (3) trading the securities of Russian government-owned, -controlled, or -affiliated entities on U.S. national securities exchanges.
The bill extends through 2031 the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996, which requires the President, with some exceptions, to impose sanctions on certain persons engaged in specified transactions related to Iran's energy sector or Iran's efforts to acquire or develop certain weapons.
The bill expands eligibility for federal tax deductions of certain educator expenses to early childhood educators providing educational or childcare services to those under age 6.
posts.meta: Ways and Means Committee · Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-CA)
posts.whatsNext: Back to the House (amendments must match exactly)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill sets up a range of sanctions and trade restrictions aimed at Russia, extends an existing law that punishes certain dealings with Iran, and widens a tax break for teachers so that it also covers some early childhood educators.

On Russia, the President must block visas and property of named individuals and organizations, including the Russian president and certain Russian military commanders. The President must also be able to raise tariffs on goods coming into the United States from a country that was among the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, up to 100% of the goods' value, if that country knowingly makes new purchases of those products after the bill becomes law.

The bill also bans three things: exporting or moving U.S.-made energy products to or within Russia, American individuals and companies making new investments in Russia or buying Russian government debt, and trading the stocks of Russian government-owned, controlled, or affiliated companies on U.S. stock exchanges.

The bill extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031. That law requires the President, with some exceptions, to impose sanctions on certain people who take part in specified deals involving Iran's energy sector or its efforts to get or develop certain weapons.

Finally, the bill extends a federal tax deduction for certain educator expenses to early childhood educators who provide educational or childcare services to children under age 6.

posts.title: Diversity Jurisdiction Inflation Adjustment Act
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Diversity Jurisdiction Inflation Adjustment Act
This bill raises the minimum amount in controversy for federal diversity jurisdiction.
Under current law, federal courts have jurisdiction over civil cases in which the monetary amount in controversy exceeds $75,000 and there is diversity of citizenship among the parties (e.g., the parties are citizens of different states).
This bill raises the minimum amount in controversy from $75,000 to $150,000 and adjusts the amount for inflation every 10 years beginning in 2030.
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text: This bill raises the amount of money a lawsuit must be worth before it can be heard in federal court based on the parties coming from different states. Right now, a case can go to federal court this way if the amount in dispute is more than $75,000. Under the bill, that threshold would rise to $150,000. Starting in 2030, the amount would also be adjusted for inflation every 10 years.

posts.title: Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026
This bill establishes processing timelines and expands claims assistance, outreach, and reporting requirements pertaining to claims for benefits under the Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) program. The PSOB program provides death, disability, and education benefits to public safety officers who are killed or injured in the line of duty and their survivors.
This bill requires the Department of Justice's Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) to notify a claimant of any missing information required to process a claim within 90 days of receiving the claim and generally requires the BJA to determine eligibility within 270 days of a completed claim.
In addition, the bill requires the BJA to use its subpoena authority to obtain information or documentation that is necessary to adjudicate a claim if a public agency fails to provide it 30 days after a request.
Under the bill, the BJA must conduct ongoing outreach to promote awareness of the PSOB program. The BJA must also report on whether a delay in processing a claim was due to the inaction of the claimant or the public agency from which information is required.
The bill requires the BJA to implement the recommendations of the Government Accountability Office (GAO) in the 2024 report, Public Safety Officers' Benefits Program: Transparency, Claims Assistance, and Program Management Improvements Needed.
Finally, the GAO must conduct an annual audit of PSOB claims that have been pending for more than one year.
posts.meta: Judiciary Committee · Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
The Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026 aims to speed up and improve the handling of claims under the Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) program. That program provides death, disability, and education benefits to public safety officers who are killed or hurt in the line of duty, and to their families.

Under the bill, the Department of Justice's Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) must tell a claimant within 90 days of receiving a claim if any information needed to process it is missing. The BJA generally must decide whether a claim is eligible within 270 days of receiving a completed claim.

If a public agency does not provide information or documents needed to decide a claim within 30 days of a request, the BJA must use its subpoena power to get them.

The BJA must also keep up ongoing outreach to make more people aware of the PSOB program. It must report on whether any delay in processing a claim was caused by the claimant or by the public agency that had to supply information.

The bill further requires the BJA to carry out the recommendations in a 2024 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on the program's transparency, claims assistance, and management. Finally, the GAO must audit each year any PSOB claims that have been pending for more than one year.

posts.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
posts.label: ⏱️ Cloture motion filed
posts.summary:
Protect College Sports Act of 2026
This bill establishes requirements for name, image, or likeness (NIL) agreements for college student athletes and provides a limited antitrust exemption for schools and conferences to pool and sell certain college sports media rights. The requirements address elements of the court-approved agreement to settle In re College Athlete NIL Litigation (i.e., House settlement).
First, the bill statutorily prohibits institutions, conferences, or interstate intercollegiate athletic associations (e.g., the National Collegiate Athletic Association [NCAA]) from restricting student athletes from entering NIL agreements (subject to specified limitations). Students must report to their institution NIL compensation greater than $600.
The bill requires agents to register with a state and caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%.
The bill also provides student athletes with one transfer without losing athletic eligibility and restricts football personnel from becoming the head football coach at a different institution during the same season.
Further, the bill prohibits institutions, conferences, or specified entities acting for the benefit of an institution from providing athletes with compensation that circumvents the limit on sharing revenue with student athletes established under the House settlement. The bill also makes the limit permanent and provides for an annual inflation adjustment.
The bill generally prohibits Division I conferences from reducing the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that a member institution must sponsor. Specifically, large institutions ($80 million or more in annual athletics revenue) must offer and maintain at least as many grant-in-aid opportunities and roster spots for sports that do not generate positive net revenue as the institution provided during academic year 2024-25. The bill provides for a waiver of this requirement under certain circumstances of financial hardship and the requirements expire nine years after the enactment of the bill.
Additionally, the bill establishes (subject to specified conditions) a limited antitrust exemption for institutions or conferences that form joint agreements to transfer their sports telecasting rights to a third party. Such an agreement requires participation from at least 75% of the institutions in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.meta: Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee · Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
posts.whatsNext: Cloture vote expected on the second session day (60 votes to advance)

aiSummaries.text:
The Protect College Sports Act of 2026 sets rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, or likeness (NIL) and gives schools and conferences a limited legal exemption to pool and sell certain sports TV and media rights. Many of its requirements follow up on a court-approved settlement in a lawsuit known as the House settlement.

Under the bill, colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations such as the NCAA generally cannot stop student athletes from signing NIL deals, though some limits apply. Students must report to their school any NIL pay greater than $600. Agents who work with athletes must register with a state, and their fees under endorsement contracts are capped at 5%.

The bill also makes some changes to athletes' eligibility and coaching. Student athletes can transfer one time without losing their eligibility to compete. Football personnel are barred from becoming the head football coach at a different school during the same season.

To prevent schools from getting around the House settlement, the bill bans payments to athletes that are designed to avoid the limit on revenue sharing with athletes. That limit becomes permanent and will rise each year to keep pace with inflation.

For Division I conferences, the bill generally stops them from cutting the number of varsity or Olympic sports teams that member schools must sponsor. Large schools, defined as those with $80 million or more in annual athletics revenue, must keep offering at least as many scholarships and roster spots in sports that do not bring in positive net revenue as they did in the 2024-25 academic year. A waiver is available in certain serious financial hardship cases. These requirements expire nine years after the bill is enacted.

Finally, the bill creates a limited antitrust exemption, subject to certain conditions, that lets schools or conferences jointly agree to transfer their sports broadcast rights to a third party. Such an agreement must include at least 75% of the schools in the Football Bowl Subdivision.

posts.title: AGOA Extension Act
posts.label: ⏱️ Cloture motion filed
posts.summary:
AGOA Extension Act
This bill extends through December 31, 2028, trade preferences that provide duty-free access to the U.S. market for most exports from eligible countries in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The bill also extends through December 31, 2031, customs user fees and merchandise processing fees.
Specifically, the bill extends through 2028 the duty-free treatment of the products of beneficiary SSA countries under the Trade Act of 1974 (specifically, the Generalized System of Preferences) and the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). (Currently, there are 32 countries eligible for AGOA.)
Additionally, the extended period applies to the following provisions of AGOA: (1) the duty-free treatment of certain apparel articles from beneficiary SSA countries; and (2) the third-country fabric provision, which allows limited amounts of apparel articles from lesser developed beneficiary SSA countries to qualify for duty-free treatment, even if the yarns and fabrics used in their production are imported from non-AGOA countries (e.g., apparel assembled in Kenya with Chinese fabrics).
The bill also provides for the refund of duties (i.e., liquidation or reliquidation of entries) on articles from eligible SSA countries that entered into the United States after September 30, 2025, and before the date of this bill's enactment. A refund request must be filed with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and must contain sufficient information for CBP to locate the entry or, if the entry cannot be located, reconstruct the entry. CBP must refund any duties previously paid with respect to the entry within 90 days.

CBP must then refund the duties previously paid on that entry within 90 days.

posts.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate with amendment (voice vote)
posts.summary:
Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 and revises programs that support research and development of drugs and other therapies to address amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig's disease) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
The bill reauthorizes
grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for scientific research on investigational drugs to prevent or treat ALS for individuals not otherwise eligible for clinical trials,
grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for research and development of therapies to prevent and treat ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases, and
a Public-Private Partnership including the FDA and NIH that supports development and regulatory review of treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
Also, the bill revises the NIH grants to require (1) the NIH, in considering grant renewal, to assess available information on the safety and efficacy of the investigational drugs; (2) grantees to promptly report available safety data from ongoing clinical trials; and (3) the NIH to determine the timeframe for enrollment in clinical trials for the investigational drugs.
Additionally, every five years, the FDA must publish a plan describing actions it will take over a five-year period to foster development of safe and effective drugs, and facilitate access to investigational drugs, for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases. Each plan must include the FDA's previous actions and recommendations for improvements.
Finally, the Government Accountability Office and the Department of Health and Human Services must report on the impacts of these grants.
posts.summaryLabel: Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate
posts.committee: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
posts.meta: Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee · Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill extends, through fiscal year 2031, several federal programs that fund research into treatments for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) and other brain and nerve diseases that worsen over time. The programs cover three areas: grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for research on experimental drugs to prevent or treat ALS for people who would not otherwise qualify for clinical trials; grants from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for developing therapies for ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases; and a public-private partnership involving the FDA and NIH that supports developing and reviewing treatments for these diseases.

The bill also changes the NIH grant rules. When deciding whether to renew a grant, the NIH must look at the available information on how safe and effective the experimental drugs are. Grant recipients must promptly report any safety data they have from ongoing clinical trials. In addition, the NIH will set the timeframe for enrolling people in clinical trials of these drugs.

Every five years, the FDA must publish a plan describing what it will do over the next five years to encourage the development of safe and effective drugs for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases, and to make experimental drugs easier to access. Each plan must include the actions the FDA took in the past and recommendations for improvement.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office and the Department of Health and Human Services must each report on the effects of these grants.

posts.title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
posts.label: ✅🏛️ Passed Senate (unanimous consent)
posts.summary:
Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill restores changes that expired in 2024 applicable to debt limits for Subchapter V (small business reorganization) and Chapter 13 (the wage earner's plan) bankruptcies.
Specifically, the bill increases the debt limit under Subchapter V from approximately $3.4 million to $7.5 million and increases the cumulative debt limit under Chapter 13 from approximately $2.1 million to $2.75 million.
The bill also applies both secured and unsecured debt towards the Chapter 13 limit. (Currently, separate limits apply to secured and unsecured debt under Chapter 13 bankruptcy.)
posts.meta: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
posts.whatsNext: To the House (if and when it takes it up)

aiSummaries.text:
This bill brings back higher debt limits for two types of bankruptcy that expired in 2024. It raises the debt limit for small business reorganization cases under Subchapter V from about $3.4 million to $7.5 million. It also raises the total debt limit for wage earner's plans under Chapter 13 from about $2.1 million to $2.75 million.

The bill changes how Chapter 13 debt is counted. Right now, separate limits apply to secured debt (debt backed by property, such as a mortgage) and unsecured debt (debt not backed by property). Under the bill, both kinds of debt count toward one combined Chapter 13 limit.
